articles.title: More Realistic Images, More Stable Editing Across 100 Rounds | Introducing Seedream 5.5
articles.description: More Realistic Images, More Stable Editing Across 100 Rounds | Introducing Seedream 5.5
articles.full_text:
Title: Seed News - ByteDance Seed Team

URL Source: https://seed.bytedance.com/en/blog/more-realistic-images-more-stable-editing-across-100-rounds-introducing-seedream-5-5

Markdown Content:
**Today, we are introducing Seedream 5.5, our next-generation image creation model.**

Image creation models are becoming part of professional visual production workflows. What matters is whether they can consistently deliver usable results that meet quality standards and deadlines while staying within budget.

We believe progress in visual intelligence should both expand creative possibilities and make professional production more reliable. This calls for expressive images, accurate content, and control over edits. With that reliability, creative teams can explore more freely and refine their ideas to their full potential.

To meet these needs, Seedream 5.5 brings three key upgrades:

*   **More stable multi-turn editing:**Preserve unedited regions at the pixel level and eliminate color shifts in those areas, while reducing detail loss and image degradation across successive edits. This supports continued work on the same image across 100 rounds of editing.

*   **Native RGBA assets with transparent backgrounds:**Directly generate images with an alpha channel, including full and partial transparency. The model carefully renders edges and transparent regions, allowing generated elements to enter downstream design workflows as standalone assets without separate background removal or edge cleanup.

*   **More realistic images and clearer text:**The model renders lighting, materials, and skin textures more naturally and reduces excessive gloss and overexposure, bringing generated images closer to real photos. Text rendering also improves significantly, with more accurate rendering of complex character shapes and densely arranged small text.

Evaluations show a substantial improvement in overall performance over the previous version. Compared with other major models, Seedream 5.5 achieves leading results in text structure and text-to-image realism.

## **Multi-turn editing with pixel-level preservation, bringing complex ideas reliably to life**

In complex, real-world creative work, each generated image can spark a new idea. The next edit brings that idea into the image, allowing the concept to develop through successive iterations.

This requires the model to carry out each new edit while reliably preserving content that does not need to change. As one output becomes the next input, small errors can accumulate over successive edits, causing detail loss and image degradation.

To address this, Seedream 5.5 uses targeted training to preserve unedited regions at the pixel level, enabling creative teams to keep refining an image through successive edits.

In this demo, we performed 100 successive edits on an image of the same person, using the previous round's output as the basis for each new edit. Even after repeated changes to clothing, accessories, and tabletop objects, the model can still make precise edits to small objects such as rings and eyeglass frames. It accounts for the subject's current pose, rendering natural contact between accessories and skin, coherent occlusion, and consistent lighting.

[Video 13](https://lf3-static.bytednsdoc.com/obj/eden-cn/lapzild-tss/ljhwZthlaukjlkulzlp/user-upload/4xfa4mw8lxj52.mp4)
Next, four floral designs demonstrate multi-turn editing across multiple objects and materials, spanning realistic flowers, still-life arrangements, journal collages, and traditional painting. Even after repeated additions and replacements of stems and decorative elements, Seedream 5.5 can still change the shape or material of a specified flower. It renders openwork lace, the sheen of beads, and the textures of stems and leaves while correctly handling occlusion between objects.

[Video 14](https://lf3-static.bytednsdoc.com/obj/eden-cn/lapzild-tss/ljhwZthlaukjlkulzlp/user-upload/4xfa4mw8ly86f.mp4)
Successive changes to an interior bring another challenge. As furniture and furnishings change, the model must keep spatial relationships consistent with the layout at each step.

In this sequence, an old study gradually becomes a colorful, imaginative space. As a box is moved around the room, the model adjusts perspective, occlusion, and cast shadows, and plausibly renders the areas that are no longer hidden. The room keeps evolving, while perspective and occlusion remain coherent at every step.

[Video 15](https://lf3-static.bytednsdoc.com/obj/eden-cn/lapzild-tss/ljhwZthlaukjlkulzlp/user-upload/4xfa4mw8lyhgf.mp4)
## **Native RGBA assets, skip background removal. Compose freely.**

Generating assets that can be arranged independently and reused across projects is an important step toward integrating image models into professional production workflows.

Seedream 5.5 introduces native RGBA generation, directly producing images with an alpha channel that supports full and partial transparency. The model preserves the subject's shape and texture while accurately rendering edges and transparent regions, so the output can be used as a standalone asset in layout, compositing, and production.

Creators can generate assets with transparent backgrounds from text descriptions or reference images. In the demo, a snowy owl spreads its wings, revealing clearly defined layers of feathers. The model carefully renders the feathers at the wingtips, the tiny gaps between them, and the outlines of the claws, preserving complex structures without the need for subsequent background removal and edge cleanup.

[Video 16](https://lf3-static.bytednsdoc.com/obj/eden-cn/lapzild-tss/ljhwZthlaukjlkulzlp/user-upload/4xfa4mw8lza1z.mp4)
Native RGBA output also supports creative compositions that bring text and visual elements together. The model can draw on the brushwork, colors, and material effects in a reference image and apply them when rendering specified text. It keeps the text accurate and legible while directly generating visual assets with transparent backgrounds.

[Video 17](https://lf3-static.bytednsdoc.com/obj/eden-cn/lapzild-tss/ljhwZthlaukjlkulzlp/user-upload/4xfa4mw8m13o4.mp4)
Assets with transparent backgrounds can also be reused across projects to make production more efficient. In the demo, a designer uses the same set of character assets as references to quickly create a series of images in different settings. The model retains the characters' defining features and textures while allowing changes to their poses, groupings, and composition. This reduces repetitive production work and makes it easier to create a cohesive series.

[Video 18](https://lf3-static.bytednsdoc.com/obj/eden-cn/lapzild-tss/ljhwZthlaukjlkulzlp/user-upload/4xfa4mw8m1xbk.mp4)
## **More realistic images, more accurate small-text rendering**

Seedream 5.5 further improves overall image quality, particularly in realism and text rendering. The model renders lighting, materials, and skin textures more naturally in realistic scenes. It also reduces excessive gloss, overexposure, and blotchy textures in some images, so the results look closer to real photos.

![Image 1: remote-media-1794189443706.png](https://lf3-static.bytednsdoc.com/obj/eden-cn/lapzild-tss/ljhwZthlaukjlkulzlp/user-upload/4xfa4mw8m2iyi.png)

In portraits, the model captures realistic skin texture in greater detail under different lighting conditions. In the first image, a young woman looks back toward the camera. Her skin texture is clearly visible, highlights blend naturally into shadow across her shoulder, and loose strands of hair catch the backlight. In the other image, a father holding a sleeping baby reclines on a sofa. Soft window light falls across his face and arms, while details in the skin and fabric remain visible in shadow, giving the scene a sense of everyday life.

![Image 2: remote-media-1794189450348.png](https://lf3-static.bytednsdoc.com/obj/eden-cn/lapzild-tss/ljhwZthlaukjlkulzlp/user-upload/4xfa4mw8m2o30.png)

The model also renders a richer range of textures and more nuanced light and shadow in scenes. Sunlight brings out the folds of a purple curtain, which casts a shadow on a rough yellow wall. As a race car speeds along a rain-soaked track, its bodywork and the wet road reflect light differently. Spray from the tires spreads behind it, partly obscuring cars in the distance and giving the scene both movement and depth.

![Image 3: remote-media-1794189452786.png](https://lf3-static.bytednsdoc.com/obj/eden-cn/lapzild-tss/ljhwZthlaukjlkulzlp/user-upload/4xfa4mw8m2pyq.png)

Seedream 5.5 improves the generation and layout of densely arranged small text, reproducing complex character shapes more accurately. On a newspaper-style page about Shakespeare, several passages of small English text sit between his portrait and an illustration of a theater. The text remains easy to read even in this compact layout.

![Image 4: remote-media-1794189461337.png](https://lf3-static.bytednsdoc.com/obj/eden-cn/lapzild-tss/ljhwZthlaukjlkulzlp/user-upload/4xfa4mw8m2wk9.png)

The blue morpho butterfly infographic shows how the model renders Chinese text at small sizes. Eight illustrated notes describe features such as the antennae, wing veins, and scales. Even in the small captions beside the close-ups, characters with many strokes are easy to read.

![Image 5: remote-media-1794189464008.png](https://lf3-static.bytednsdoc.com/obj/eden-cn/lapzild-tss/ljhwZthlaukjlkulzlp/user-upload/4xfa4mw8m2ymh.png)

## **Seedream 5.5 evaluations: substantial gains in overall performance, leading results in text structure and text-to-image realism**

To evaluate performance in professional production, we tested the model across six use cases: e-commerce, marketing, film and television, gaming, office productivity, and fashion design. Evaluations were conducted on the MagicArena platform, with experienced image-generation evaluators assessing output quality and usability.

Compared with Seedream 5.0 Pro, Seedream 5.5 improved both quality scores and usability rates across all six use cases. In film and television and in office productivity, usability rates were more than twice those of the previous version.

![Image 6](https://lf3-static.bytednsdoc.com/obj/eden-cn/lapzild-tss/ljhwZthlaukjlkulzlp/user-upload/4xfa4mw8ql1vo.jpg)

_Seedream 5.5 performance across production use cases. Left: usability rate. Right: mean opinion score (MOS)._

In separate evaluations of text structure and realism, experts compared pairs of generated images, scoring their preferences using GSB (Good/Same/Bad) across both text-to-image and image-to-image tasks. Seedream 5.5 received positive GSB scores against the previous version in all four comparisons, reaching +55.62% for realism in image-to-image tasks. Compared with leading models such as GPT Image 2.5 Sunburst and Nano Banana 2.1, Seedream 5.5 leads in text structure across both tasks and shows a substantial advantage in text-to-image realism.

![Image 7: Text structure and realism evaluations. The chart shows Seedream 5.5's GSB scores in text-to-image and image-to-image tasks.](https://lf3-static.bytednsdoc.com/obj/eden-cn/lapzild-tss/ljhwZthlaukjlkulzlp/user-upload/4xfa4mw8m342o.jpg)

_Text structure and realism evaluations. The chart shows Seedream 5.5's GSB scores in text-to-image and image-to-image tasks._

Improvements in text rendering are also reflected in lower text corruption rates. In evaluations covering Chinese and English, including densely arranged small text, Seedream 5.5's severe text corruption rate fell to 0.4%, while its minor text corruption rate fell to 1.7%. Both rates are substantially lower than in the previous version and are also among the best in comparisons with leading models.

![Image 8](https://lf3-static.bytednsdoc.com/obj/eden-cn/lapzild-tss/ljhwZthlaukjlkulzlp/user-upload/4xfa4mw8qmvhl.jpg)

_Text rendering quality. Left: severe text corruption rate. Right: minor text corruption rate. Lower values indicate fewer errors._

## **Summary and outlook**

Seedream 5.5 improves image quality and makes multi-turn editing more stable, while native RGBA output expands how generated assets can be used. These capabilities help creative teams refine their work and reuse existing assets, better meeting professional production requirements for quality, reliability, and efficiency.

Looking ahead, we will support more complex contextual inputs and creative instructions, while continuing to improve the model's performance on professional tasks. Guided by real production needs in film and television, e-commerce, advertising, and design, we will also expand its use in agent workflows and continue exploring more general visual intelligence. A Pro version of the Seedream 5.5 series will follow. Stay tuned.

People should always be in control of the future.

OpenAI is against the notion that it would be acceptable for people to be relegated to a role of doing things that “AI systems think makes sense to reward in humans”.

People should not cede control of the future to superintelligence, and that requirement should ultimately constrain AI progress.

articles.description:
New Anthropic research: progress on provable inference for large language models.

Here, we introduce FlashProve. Building on established cryptographic techniques, FlashProve allows developers to verify whether a given response came from a given AI model. It’s substantially more efficient than prior open-source methods for doing so. 

These proofs have a range of applications. They can, for instance, make it harder for attackers to hijack a chat, or enable safety evaluators to verify that the model they’re testing is the same one being served to customers.

For our full write-up, see here: https://t.co/OIZWPb6QZa

Further progress in provable inference will likely be an important part of improving trust in AI deployment. To that end, we're open-sourcing FlashProve’s code, here: https://t.co/7ky3Ir8V06

We’re grateful to our collaborators: Alessandro Chiesa, @GiacomoFenzi, @gwberg95, @miranda__christ, Rahul Dalal (https://t.co/pjWKLHWXyz) and Ben Mayer (@transmissions11).
articles.linked_content:
Title: Progress on provable inference for large language models

URL Source: https://www.anthropic.com/research/provable-inference

Published Time: 2026-11-02T00:00:00.000Z

Markdown Content:
_Roy Rinberg (Anthropic), Alex Allain (Anthropic); Alessandro Chiesa (EPFL, StarkWare), Miranda Christ (MIT, RESI), Rahul Dalal (Anthropic STEM Fellows Program, Succinct), Giacomo Fenzi (EPFL), Ben Mayer (Anthropic Fellows Program, MIT), Guy Weissenberg (EPFL)_

## Executive summary

When you talk to a friend in person, you have many ways to know it is really them: you can see them, hear them, shake their hand. When you talk to an AI model, you have almost none. A user querying a model today cannot check that the responses came from the specific model that a developer claims is responding, as opposed to one secretly substituted in by a routing service for cost reasons, or even by an attacker who has tampered with the token stream. Judging from the model’s output alone is unreliable, even if it produces high-quality responses. Cryptographic proofs of inference solve this problem: they let a model provider commit to a model and then prove that each response was produced by that model. Such proofs could enable applications ranging from consumer products to internal security, and could contribute to a toolkit for verifying compliance with AI pacing requirements.

Specifically, we have made progress on a powerful type of cryptographic proof known as a “zkSNARK”, which is uniquely fit for **provable inference** (owing to its strong hiding and efficiency properties). In this post, we share some of that progress, primarily through a system we call FlashProve. A brief technical summary is as follows:

1.   Claude has produced improvements on zkSNARKs for inference, building a system that is substantially faster than prior open-source systems. 
    1.   For a large model (Llama 4 Maverick, 400B-parameter mixture of experts), a single H100 GPU generates proofs at around 110 tokens/second, with a proof size of ~19 MB per 1,024-token request, when in 4-bit quantized weights, using integer arithmetic in prefill. This is ~70-95x the GPU time of running the model itself on vLLM, a common open-source library. 
    2.   Prior open-source systems are orders of magnitude slower, as we discuss in [section 6](https://www.anthropic.com/research/provable-inference#prior-work). Claude found novel ways to apply state-of-the-art tools in the cryptography and security literature, while relying on well-established design principles for cryptographic proof systems. The commitment to the model, and subsequent inference proofs, hide the weights of the model; hiding the architecture of the model is not a goal of this system.

2.   Claude is good at optimization, but often makes decisions that are hard to evaluate, especially in large complex systems. We counter this by providing top-level auditable statements in Lean (a formal verification language) for the claimed security guarantees.

Today we are releasing five artifacts:

*   The current blog post, which outlines our system and its potential applications;
*   A [technical report](https://www.anthropic.com/document/flashprove-technical-report) explaining the details of our system;
*   A (Claude-written) [protocol specification](https://github.com/anthropics/FlashProve/blob/main/paper/paper.pdf) document;
*   [Executable code](https://github.com/anthropics/FlashProve) that includes: a [prover](https://github.com/anthropics/FlashProve/tree/main/prover) and two verifiers, a [fast verifier](https://github.com/anthropics/FlashProve/tree/main/verifier) in C++, and a [provably correct verifier](https://github.com/anthropics/FlashProve/tree/main/tools/lean-verify) in Lean; and
*   [Lean proofs](https://github.com/anthropics/FlashProve/tree/main/lean) for the top level mathematical statements, along with an [interactive visualizer](https://github.com/anthropics/FlashProve/blob/main/lean/STATEMENTS.html) of the Lean theorems to aid with auditing.

We release our code, Lean proofs, and documentation under the Apache 2.0 license.[1](https://www.anthropic.com/research/provable-inference#footnote-1) This research post is meant to share intermediate progress, and not a completed research agenda. We are sharing this explicitly with the goal that others look at what we have done, take it, and improve it.

## Introduction

When a user sends a request to an AI model, today they have no way of knowing for certain that the model they selected is the one that generated the response. For everyday uses, in which users mostly care about the output and not necessarily which specific model produced it, this is a less pressing concern. But there are several cases where such assurance would be useful. For example, independent evaluators who test AI models before and after release need to know that the model they are evaluating is the model being served. Clients who use a model through a third-party routing service want assurance that the tokens came from the model they paid for. And if a cyberattacker modifies the token stream while pretending to be a given model, a user has no way to detect it from the output alone.

However, enabling verification of model responses is challenging. Most frontier models’ weights are kept private, and even if the user had access to the weights, checking that a given response was produced by a model with those weights would involve running the model, which requires computational resources far beyond what a typical user (or even evaluator) can afford.

The goal of _provable inference_ (PI) is to enable a user with limited computational resources and without any information about the weights to verify that a response came from the requested model. PI is motivated both by a desire to increase customer trust in AI providers, and—because it can be used to provide assurances to independent evaluators and allows providers to demonstrate that they are meeting certain commitments and legal obligations—it also has implications for pacing the frontier of AI development and for AI regulation.

One way to implement PI is via a cryptographic object called a _zero-knowledge succinct argument:_ the model provider sends, along with the claimed response, a short _proof_(say, a few megabytes) that the user can _quickly_ verify (ideally, in seconds on a CPU). If the claimed response deviates from the specified model, the user’s check will fail. Importantly, cryptographic techniques ensure that the proof reveals _nothing_ about the model’s weights.

Today, we release FlashProve: an **open-source performant prototype for provable inference**. For a 400B-parameter mixture-of-experts model (Llama 4 Maverick, 4-bit quantization), we show that a single H100 GPU generates proofs at over 100 tokens/second, with proof size of ~19 MB per 1,024-token request (~70-95 times the GPU time that vLLM, a common open-source library, takes to process prompts of the same length).

The release comes with executable code, Lean formalization, and a technical description of the protocol. Our aim is twofold: (i) accelerating and facilitating the development of provable inference; and (ii) demonstrating that zero-knowledge succinct arguments are practical for provable inference.

We believe that this progress has meaningful implications for security, in **pacing AI development**, in **providing AI customers with integrity guarantees**, in **facilitating tooling for auditors and regulators**, and more.

## Trust challenges in AI proliferation

The development of artificial intelligence and its growing role in our digital infrastructure and economy raises [trust challenges](https://arxiv.org/abs/2004.07213) that AI providers must answer. Addressing these and other challenges is facilitated by relying on tools for _provable inference (PI)._

Tools for PI include hardware approaches, software approaches, or a combination of both. Here, we focus on a software-only approach: a cryptographic tool known as a “zkSNARK” (_zero-knowledge succinct argument of knowledge_). Informally, a zkSNARK is a system allowing a _prover_ to convince a _verifier_, by way of a short “certificate”, that a given computation was executed correctly; crucially, the certificate is _zero-knowledge_ in that it reveals no information beyond what is implied by the computation’s correctness and is _succinct_ in that it’s exponentially faster to verify compared to the proved computation.

Below we outline several challenges and how zkSNARKs help in addressing them.

### Challenge 1: pacing

Some proposals to [regulate](https://thefuturesociety.org/international-ai-verification) and [pace](https://darioamodei.com/post/we-must-pace-the-frontier) AI development rely on [monitoring hardware and how it is used](https://arxiv.org/abs/2402.08797). For example, a provider might be required to [devote its hardware to inference](https://arxiv.org/abs/2506.15867) rather than to training a powerful new model. The provider might try to cheat by serving cheaper models or using compute in an unexpected way, freeing up resources for training. How can a regulator reliably ensure that the hardware is used for inference?

_How zkSNARKs can help:_ The regulator can ask the provider for certificates covering the inference requests served in a given period. The certificates must show that the requests were generated by the claimed model. A malicious provider cannot satisfy this request unless its hardware was genuinely serving the right model. Using a zkSNARK, the regulator can check that the provider claims are valid without needing the elaborate hardware setup that the provider may have, and at the same time the provider has the guarantee that the regulator does not learn proprietary model information.[2](https://www.anthropic.com/research/provable-inference#footnote-2) We note that although this verifies that the hardware is serving inference, it does not establish that the hardware is not, e.g., training on the side.

### Challenge 2: tamper detection

As AI models grow more valuable, the servers that run them become [prime targets](https://www.rand.org/pubs/research_reports/RRA2849-1.html). An attacker or rogue agent may [compromise an inference server](https://www.wiz.io/blog/nvidia-triton-cve-2025-23319-vuln-chain-to-ai-server) to exfiltrate the weights, serve users malicious responses (such as delivering malware to the user’s computer), and more, all while [hiding among genuine responses](https://arxiv.org/abs/2511.02620). The adversary need not be external. As models become capable of improving and deploying themselves, a more advanced model could run in place of the one that was authorized and present itself as the weaker model, so as to avoid the classifiers and monitoring that would apply to it. In both cases the question is the same: how can a company be sure of _which weights_ are actually running on its servers? In our [Frontier Safety Roadmap](https://www.anthropic.com/responsible-scaling-policy/roadmap), Anthropic set a [public goal](https://www.anthropic.com/responsible-scaling-policy/roadmap#moonshot-r-d-projects) to produce a prototype for verifying inference traffic: “_We will develop a prototype by September 30, 2026 of provable inference, a technique for reliably, provably ‘signing’ AI model outputs in a way that makes them attributable to a specific set of model weights._” As stated in our RSP updates, we met that goal through a separate but related project, which signs our inference traffic and recomputes inference on a trusted server; the work in this blog post pursues the same objective by a different method.[3](https://www.anthropic.com/research/provable-inference#footnote-3)

_How zkSNARKs can help:_ The provider can require a valid zkSNARK from the server on every response. A proof is bound to a specific commitment to the weights, so it certifies not just that _some_ model produced the response but that the _committed_ model did. An attacker who compromises a server, or a model that substitutes itself for another, must then produce valid proofs for the expected weights to avoid detection, which they cannot do. The user may receive the proofs as well, since they leak no internal information (by zero knowledge) and are cheap to check (by succinctness); this limits what an attacker can accomplish through the inference API.

### Challenge 3: text provenance

One may want to prove that considerable effort went into understanding/analyzing something. For example, a developer might claim that their software library was scanned for vulnerabilities by a frontier cybersecurity model, or a company might claim that its business plan was given the go-ahead by an appropriate model. How can a user verify these claims? The user might not have the resources to run the model itself (or they might not have the clearance to do so). Even publishing the chat logs gives no absolute guarantees; a developer might in theory fake them, generating them not with a frontier model but instead with a [cheaper one](https://arxiv.org/abs/2504.04715) or a [degraded version](https://kimi.com/blog/kimi-vendor-verifier). In general, how can users verify that they are being served by [their chosen model](https://arxiv.org/abs/2410.20247)?

_How zkSNARKs can help:_ The provider can append, along with each response, a zkSNARK proving that the output was produced by the claimed model on the given input. Succinctness lets the user check this certificate quickly, without specialized hardware, and zero-knowledge assures the provider that the user learns nothing about the proprietary weights. This complements [existing mechanisms](https://arxiv.org/abs/2511.20621) for verifying which model produced a response.

For example, in a world where exploits are being found regularly, prior to releasing new code a model provider could provide the code-developer a Proof-of-Failure that the model-provider spent at least X tokens on a specific model, and did not achieve a specific result (for example, this specific model did not find any bugs in a specific patch, after trying for at least 1M tokens).

### Challenge 4: model approval

Regulation might require providers to [serve only models approved as safe](https://arxiv.org/abs/2307.03718), rather than models deemed a cybersecurity or safety risk. A provider might have an incentive to circumvent this, since risky models might outperform competitors or be cheaper to serve. How can a regulator ensure that [only approved models are served](https://arxiv.org/abs/2507.15916)?

_How zkSNARKs can help:_ The regulator can require the provider to attach a zkSNARK to its responses, enforcing the use of approved models. The proof binds each request to the used model, so it will not verify if the provider is using an unapproved model. The regulator can check this in a lightweight way thanks to succinctness without requiring to re-execute each request.

_A note on PI from trusted hardware._ Prior work often focuses on _trusted execution environments_ to achieve PI. These are hardware-based solutions that provide privacy and attestation that rely on the manufacturer producing tamper-resistant hardware. In this research, our focus is on software-only cryptographic solutions whose security and privacy relies on the hardness of computational problems. Even in the face of compromised environments (hardware, operating system and more) an adversary cannot produce a invalid proof without breaking a computationally infeasible problem. Trusted hardware and cryptography are complementary approaches with different guarantees and tradeoffs. Both will play a role in addressing the above trust challenges.

## Our system: FlashProve

FlashProve is a system for provable inference of large Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) language models. More details are in our [technical report](https://www.anthropic.com/document/flashprove-technical-report); here we outline the system.

FlashProve involves two parties: the model provider (the _prover_) and a user (the _verifier_). It is split into two phases:

*   In the **offline phase**, the prover publishes a _commitment_ to the model weights, which is a short fingerprint to pin down _one_ exact choice of weights while the weights themselves remain hidden. The later inference claims will be checked against that commitment, i.e., the weight model committed to in this phase.
*   In the **online phase**, upon requests from the verifier (i.e., prompts and the corresponding output tokens), the prover produces a proof file proving the following statement:

_The committed model produces these output tokens when evaluated._

Anyone who holds the commitment, the prompt, and the reply can check it, without the weights and with limited compute power, and be convinced that the committed weights, run on this prompt, produce exactly these tokens.

### Guarantees

A proof file satisfies the following “completeness” and “soundness” properties:

*   **A proof file is accepted if it is honest (completeness).**An honest prover's proof is accepted by the verifier.
*   **A proof file cannot be forged (soundness).** It is effectively impossible (i.e., tantamount to breaking widely believed cryptographic assumptions) to produce a valid proof of a false statement, so the verifier does not have to trust the prover.

Completeness and soundness alone can be achieved by a computationally powerful verifier that knows the model weights (evaluate the model on the prompt and check whether the result matches the response). The next two properties are what makes the system non-trivial.

*   **A proof file reveals nothing beyond the statement (zero-knowledge).** The verifier learns _nothing_ about the weights, the intermediate values of the computation, or which experts ran at every layer. The model architecture (excluding the weights) is not hidden.
*   **A proof file is small and cheap to check (succinctness).** The attested computation is a run of a 400B-parameter (about 232 GB for a quantized version) model on an H100 GPU, while the verifier receives a proof file of about 19 MB that takes seconds to check on a 24-core CPU. An auditor, or a user with far less hardware than the provider, can check proof files without access to elaborate infrastructure.

### Evaluation

We measured an implementation of the protocol on [Llama 4 Maverick](https://huggingface.co/meta-llama/Llama-4-Maverick-17B-128E-Instruct) (a 400B-parameter mixture of experts, with ~17B parameters used per token), using the publicly available 4-bit weights. Each verifier request is a window of 1,024 tokens, and each proof checks one token. The prover runs on a server with a single H100 and 24 CPU cores, and the verifier on a CPU.

*   **Prover.** The prover runs on a server with a single H100 and 24 CPU cores. The _offline phase_ runs once per model and takes about 39 minutes. (For technical reasons we discuss in the [technical report](https://www.anthropic.com/document/flashprove-technical-report), the resulting commitment is good for about 16 million requests, after which the provider has to commit again.) The _online phase_, on a batch of 24 requests, takes the prover about 223 seconds, which is 110 tokens per second, and each proof is 18.78 MB.
*   **Verifier.** The verifier runs on the client's CPU. It needs no GPU and only has access to a commitment to the weights. The client downloads the commitment, ~6.5 MB in all, and then one proof per request. Checking a proof takes 17 seconds on 24 threads (and 21 seconds on a single thread), including the offline phase's checks.

Comparison with plain inference: We ran [vLLM](https://vllm.ai/), a widely used inference engine, with the FP8 release of the same model on eight H100s, and found that, per GPU, proving a batch of 24 requests takes about 72 times longer than vLLM takes to process the same 24 requests at once (66 to 77 across runs), and about 94 times longer when vLLM runs at the highest load we

articles.description:
We’re sharing how our biology research team worked with Claude to map the first 3D structure of a vault particle from bacterial life.

Vault particles are a longstanding mystery. They are barrel-shaped objects, among the largest protein structures found in our cells. They were first discovered by Leonard Rome and Nancy Kedersha in 1986, but their function remains unknown.

With Claude, we’ve found results that might bring us closer to solving that mystery.

Until now, vaults were only known in the cells of complex things like animals and plants. We have shown that similar proteins from bacteria (and the viruses that infect them) can also assemble into vaults. Finding the structures in these simpler forms of life may make it easier to investigate their function in our own cells.

For our life sciences team, the project was also a demonstration of the potential (and the limitations) of using AI to accelerate science.

In our full piece, we discuss how Claude was able to dramatically speed up some stages—manually determining the vault particle’s structure would have taken weeks to months of painstaking work, but here it took days. We also discuss how Claude made some simple mistakes along the way, and how we collaborated with our machine learning researchers to address them.

Read more: https://t.co/KowVVCSPp8
articles.linked_content:
Title: Investigating vault particles with Claude

URL Source: https://www.anthropic.com/research/investigating-vault-particles-with-claude

Published Time: 2026-11-04T00:00:00.000Z

Markdown Content:
> _We’re sharing another finding from [Anthropic’s biology research lab](https://www.anthropic.com/research/claude-discovers-novel-enzyme-system): the first 3D structure of a vault particle found in prokaryotic cells. Vaults are large, hollow barrels of protein found in cells across the tree of life, and their function is still unknown. Below, we describe how Claude helped at each step of this research: searching across sequence literature, optimizing a method of isolating particles, and mapping the vault’s structure. More information is [in our preprint](https://www.biorxiv.org/content/10.64898/2026.11.04.764334v1), which we’ve submitted to bioRxiv; we’ll update the link as soon as it goes live._

Biological cells were first detected in 1665, but more than three and a half centuries later, much of how they work remains unknown. Until relatively recently, [the existence of some crucial components](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/12360195/), let alone [their function](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3184113/), was controversial. Even today, more than a third of the roughly 4,400 genes in one of the most comprehensively studied cells, the bacterium _E. coli_, [remain poorly understood](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6412132/). Another such enigma is the _vault particle_.

A vault particle is a large, hollow protein shell found in nearly all the cells in our body. [It was discovered in 1986](https://rupress.org/jcb/article-abstract/103/3/699/13490/Isolation-and-characterization-of-a-novel?redirectedFrom=fulltext) by Leonard Rome and Nancy Kedersha, but its function remains elusive. At roughly three times the mass of a ribosome, it’s one of the largest known molecular complexes in eukaryotes—organisms with complex cells, such as mammals (as opposed to simple, usually single-celled “prokaryotes,” such as bacteria). Vaults take their name from their shape. When observed under an electron microscope, the ribbed shell reminded Dr. Rome and Dr. Kedersha of the vaulted ceiling of a cathedral. In mammals, the shell is made of 78 copies of the major vault protein, arranged as two identical halves joined at the middle.

Vaults are [found across most of the eukaryotic tree](https://doi.org/10.1093/gbe/evt113), from slime molds to humans, so scientists believe that they must do something useful. Researchers have proposed various functions, including [transporting molecules between the nucleus and cytoplasm](https://doi.org/10.1242/jcs.106.1.23), [protecting cells from toxic compounds such as cancer drugs](https://doi.org/10.1038/nm0695-578), and [supporting innate immunity](https://doi.org/10.1126/science.1142311), but none of these proposals have been conclusively confirmed. Other studies have shown that [mice lacking vaults still survive](https://doi.org/10.1128/MCB.24.12.5314-5323.2004), which suggests that vaults may be necessary only under specific environmental conditions. Still, the question remains: why would evolution retain something so large if it didn’t have an important function?

Interested in whether Claude could help make progress on this long-standing open problem, our biology research team has been investigating vaults. We haven’t yet determined their biological function, but we did find that many more vault proteins across the tree of life, including those in prokaryotes and the bacteriophages that infect them, can assemble into complete vault-like particles. Related proteins had [already been found](https://www.biorxiv.org/content/10.1101/2023.11.10.566534v1.abstract) in the genomes of both prokaryotes and phages, but to our knowledge no one had shown that they assemble into vaults.

A vault in a prokaryotic cell gives researchers a simpler system to study. Compared with mammalian cells, bacteria are quick to grow, which makes it easier to investigate where vaults came from, what their basic structure looks like, and what, if anything, they contain. Studying the bacterial relatives of human proteins has been informative before. Bacterial versions of [cGAS–STING signaling](https://doi.org/10.1038/s41586-019-1605-5), [gasdermins](https://doi.org/10.1126/science.abj8432), and [viperins](https://doi.org/10.1038/s41586-020-2762-2) revealed the microbial origins of these human immune defenses. In those cases, their function in humans was already known. For vaults it is not, and their prokaryotic relatives may help reveal it.

Here, we describe how we uncovered the molecular structure of a vault from a _bacteriophage_. Bacteriophages are viruses that infect bacteria. Like all viruses, they hijack their host cells to make their proteins, so this vault would be built inside a bacterium, a prokaryotic cell. The vault is built from 96 copies of a single protein, compared with 78 in human vaults. By duplicating part of the protein, we engineered the vault to be even larger. Together, these results shed light on how such complexes assemble and suggest how they could be adapted for [biotechnology](https://www.science.org/doi/10.1126/science.adz9353)—for example, as [nanocapsules for delivering enzymes](https://www.pnas.org/doi/abs/10.1073/pnas.0500929102).

This work also demonstrates our team’s wider aim: to speed up research in fundamental biology by building Claude into every step of the process. Under our direction, Claude searched protein databases, designed the DNA constructs, optimized the isolation method, and processed the microscopy data. As a result, a vault purification that conventionally takes three days took us about 90 minutes, and a first structural model was ready 34 hours later, which we estimate would normally have taken us weeks.

Despite this progress, there is still much to be learned about these perplexing structures. When we shared the structure with Dr. Rome, whom we brought on to advise us on this research, he said:

> Figuring out the function of vaults is still enormously challenging. I am pleased that Anthropic has so much good data. Now, other people will be working on this problem … The broadness of Anthropic’s finding[s] suggests that it is going to be a complicated function and an interesting ride.

Our lab is releasing these findings early to continue to show the scientific community how Claude can be used for discovery. You can read more about our results and methods [in our preprint](https://www.biorxiv.org/content/10.64898/2026.11.04.764334v1), and we will be releasing the structures and additional data soon.

## A vault-like structure in prokaryotes

We uncovered the vault structure using cryo-electron microscopy (cryo-EM), in which many copies of a particle are flash-frozen and imaged with an electron beam, before being combined into a single 3D model. The vault is built from 96 copies (48 copies per half) of a single phage protein, which we call L05, with a combined mass of about 9.5 [megadaltons](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dalton_(unit)). By contrast, the mammalian version has 39 copies per half. The phage-derived vault is also shorter and wider: roughly 54 nanometers long and 45 wide, compared with 67 by 40 in mammals. Despite being shorter, it encloses about 25% more volume because it is more spherical. The protein chain that makes up its wall is built from seven repeating segments stacked end to end, rather than the nine in mammalian vaults, and its end caps are flatter. It’s among the largest protein shells ever identified in prokaryotes.

One notable feature of its structure is how the caps close. A wall 48 copies around must narrow toward the pole, and it does so in three steps, like a tiered dome. In every group of three neighboring copies, one ends at the first step, one at the second, and one continues to the tip. The three copies are identical along the wall, but take different shapes (conformations) in the cap.

Given that we can make this vault in the lab and isolate it quickly, we also experimented with altering its structure to learn more about how these proteins assemble. Working with Claude, we made 15 altered versions of the protein, most with changes at the points where neighboring copies touch. Some single changes near the cap were enough to prevent the shell from closing: in place of sealed vaults we saw open, rosette-like particles, which shows that this region is needed to seal the shell.

We also tried making the vault even bigger. Ordinarily, the wall is built from seven repeating segments. When we copied two of them, giving the protein nine—the same number as in the human vault—it assembled into even larger vault particles, increasing the enclosed volume by approximately 20%. These experiments demonstrate how vaults could have changed size over their evolutionary history by duplicating pieces of their own wall without disrupting how they assemble.

## Finding, isolating, and mapping a new vault with Claude

Part of the reason vaults have remained unexplained for 40 years is that they are [missing from the organisms biologists rely on most](https://doi.org/10.1093/gbe/evt113) for genetic experiments, including baker’s yeast, fruit flies, and nematode worms. In mice, which do have vaults, animals that are bred without [a vault partner protein](https://doi.org/10.1128/MCB.24.12.5314-5323.2004) or [the vault RNA](https://doi.org/10.1261/rna.080161.124) develop normally, leaving no obvious defect to follow up. In recent years, bioinformaticians [identified distant relatives](https://doi.org/10.1101/872010) of the vault protein in prokaryotes, but it wasn’t clear whether these proteins formed vaults.

Our team set out to answer that question. The research required several steps: surveying genetic sequences to find where vault proteins occur across the tree of life, producing and isolating the most promising candidates to test whether they actually assemble into vault-like particles, and determining the structure of one of the particles to see how its chains fit together.

We began by using [Claude Science](https://claude.com/product/claude-science) to search for the vault protein’s relatives across a database of about 15 billion predicted proteins. They turned out to be rare but widely distributed, present in 29 major groups (phyla) of bacteria and four of archaea (the other main group of prokaryotes) but in less than 1% of species with a sequenced genome. We then chose 44 of these proteins and tested each in [a cell-free system](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cell-free_system) to see which genes yielded full-length protein and how much. We chose the proteins, and Claude turned each protein sequence into DNA tailored to the host cell, added the control sequences that switch a gene on, and prepared the designs for ordering. We moved the best performers into living _E. coli_ bacteria, where 15 of 24 produced soluble protein.

Next, we needed to isolate the particles. The conventional method, developed for eukaryotic vaults, spins the sample through a tube of increasingly dense sugar and takes approximately three days. To speed this up, we decided to try size-exclusion chromatography. In this process, the sample flows through a column of porous beads. In a process called fractionation, small molecules get stuck in the pores, while the vaults, which are too big to enter, come out first, in what’s known as the void volume.

Claude first argued against taking the chromatography approach, because clumps of misfolded protein come out in that same void volume. We went ahead anyway, and Claude helped make it work by recommending a specific column as well as methods to track the vault protein and check whether particles had formed. Claude then proposed loading the contents of ruptured cells straight onto the column with no purification beforehand. We were reluctant at first because these columns are expensive, and the raw contents of ruptured _E. coli_ cells can clog them or cause contamination. But we were willing to test an unconventional idea, and it worked.

We are not [the first group to isolate vaults on sizing columns](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/30036602/), but our optimized method takes about 90 minutes from cells to microscopy grid instead of days. Under an electron microscope, seven of the 15 proteins had assembled into vault-like particles.

Cryo-EM confirmed the vault shape for four of those seven, two from phages and two from bacteria. We chose one of the phage proteins, L05, for the detailed structure described above because it was among the best at forming complete, closed particles. Determining a biomolecular structure often takes weeks or months of manual work with specialized software. We directed Claude through the whole process. Working in an internal multi-agent harness with access to internal compute resources, Claude set up an open-source processing software (RELION) and ran each step, while we advised on the analysis decisions. A first full model was ready in 34 hours, and the final maps were ready about a week after processing began.

Claude also pointed out a feature of the structure we can’t yet explain. A pocket partway up each of the 96 protein copies holds a small molecule that shows up clearly in the map but that we haven’t been able to identify. Claude found that its shape resembles coenzyme A, a common helper molecule that cells use to shuttle chemical groups around. If it is coenzyme A, or something similar, it would be an early hint at a possible function.

## A new way of doing science

For us, this was a dramatically different way of doing science. None of us had worked with a protein assembly this large, and we had limited experience in structural biology. We took the project on anyway, because Claude could make up for what we didn’t know and rapidly perform analyses that would otherwise have taken us much longer.

In under four months, we screened dozens of candidate vaults, prepared samples for the microscope, and solved the first vault structure found in prokaryotes. Most of this work could be achieved by a typical lab with access to existing Claude products. Only the cryo-EM analysis, which used hundreds of GPUs in parallel to save time, required more computing resources than might be available to an academic institution.

Working this way also showed us where Claude needed improvement. A protocol it wrote called for a growth medium containing an additive that interferes with getting DNA into cells, which set the project back by two weeks. Early in the cryo-EM processing, it skipped a standard step and produced a flawed map blended with its mirror image, and we told it to stop improvising (“Please let’s do normal things unless they don’t work”).

We have used what we’ve learned to inform Claude’s development. We shared our lab notes with the ML researchers who train Claude, so they could see where the model went wrong. This has informed the kind of data Claude learns from. Over the course of the project, Claude got much better at these tasks as new models arrived, making seemingly fewer errors in DNA construct design and better identifying potential pitfalls in experiments. In areas we knew well, we caught mistakes quickly, but they cost us time in areas we didn’t. Overall, we found that the benefits of working this way far outweighed the drawbacks, and Claude has become integral to our work.

So far, we have made these vaults only in _E. coli_, and have yet to test whether they form in the bacteria and phages where they’re naturally found. More work is needed to determine the function of these particles, and our work only deepens the mystery. As Dr. Rome put it:

> Will we find out that they are all doing the same thing? Or will we see an evolutionary development of vault function? Maybe they are doing the same thing as human vaults, and that is also very interesting.

We will continue our research into the function of vaults, and will share more as this work progresses.

## Work with us

We are releasing the details of our work [in our preprint](https://www.biorxiv.org/content/10.64898/2026.11.04.764334v1). If you have an idea for what these vaults might be doing, or a system in which to test it, we would like to hear from you: [mdurrant[at]anthropic.com](mailto:mdurrant@anthropic.com), [nicholasp[at]anthropic.com](mailto:nicholasp@anthropic.com).
